subQuestions.questionText: Why are markets reluctant (unwilling) to produce public goods?
subQuestions.memoText:
Memo answer (2 x 2 marks):
- Provision of public goods is not profitable, which may discourage private businesses.
- Public goods are non-excludable and consumption cannot be confined only to those who paid for them.
- There is no way of measuring how much a person consumes a public good and therefore no basis to establish a market price.
- High start-up capital is needed to provide public goods, which private businesses may not have.
- Public goods are non-rivalry â€” consumption by one person does not reduce consumption by another, hence the market cannot determine a price.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly discuss immobility of factors of production and imperfect competition as causes of market failure. (2 x 4)
subQuestions.memoText:
Memo answer (2 x 4 marks; max 4 each):

Immobility of factors of production (Max 4):
- Factors of production are very often immobile and take time to move from one place to another.
- The supply of skilled labour/entrepreneurs cannot be increased because of the time it takes to be trained or educated.
- Land and physical capital, such as factory buildings or infrastructure such as telephone lines, cannot be reallocated easily.
- Structural changes (e.g. switching from plastic to paper packets) might take time for workers to adjust.
- Technological changes may need workers to be flexible and willing to update their skills throughout their life.

Imperfect competition (Max 4):
- Competition in market economies is limited by the power of certain producers to prevent new businesses from entering the market.
- Barriers to entry are created because of advertising, lack of capital and the controlling of resources.
- The imperfect market does not allow for price negotiations.
- Advertising is used to promote producer dominance which encourages consumers to buy existing products.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(Allocate a maximum of 4 marks for a mere listing of facts/examples.)

subQuestions.questionText: How can an exit of firms in a perfect market affect the economy?
subQuestions.memoText:
Memo answer (8 marks):
- There will be a decrease in competition due to limited number of firms in the market.
- Prices of goods and services are likely to increase because of a decrease in supply.
- Unemployment levels will increase as some businesses shut down their operations.
- The aggregate demand for goods and services will decrease due to a decrease in employment levels.
- The remaining businesses may enjoy economic profit due to an increase in prices.
- Government will collect less revenue due to reduced number of firms in the economy.
- Consumers will have less access to goods and services to choose from.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(Allocate a maximum of 2 marks for a mere listing of facts/examples.)

- Businesses may increase the price of goods and services in advance to protect their profit margins.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

- Tourist activities such as destruction of coral reefs, vegetation and dunes may lead to direct environmental stress.
- Migration of people from rural to urban areas results in increased urban densities, which cause stress on the environment.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly discuss household consumption and government expenditure as causes of demand-pull inflation. (2 x 4)
subQuestions.memoText:
Memo answer (2 x 4 marks):

Household consumption:
- A decrease in personal income tax will result in households having more disposable income to spend on goods and services.
- Lower interest rates will result in credit becoming easily available, leading to higher disposable income, thus increasing demand for goods and services.
- Less savings will result in increased consumption of goods and services.

Government expenditure:
- Government expenditure on infrastructure requires high amounts of production inputs and labour, which stimulate demand for goods and services.
- An increase in consumption expenditure by government creates demand-pull inflation if the corresponding supply does not increase.
- An increase in social spending programmes such as the Expanded Public Works Programme (EPWP) without a corresponding increase in supply will stimulate demand-pull inflation.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(Allocate a maximum of 4 marks for a mere listing of facts/examples.)

subQuestions.questionText: Why is tourism in developing countries important in alleviating poverty?
subQuestions.memoText:
Memo answer (8 marks):
- It is a source of foreign exchange and job creation as tourism benefits labour-intensive industries.
- The taxing of tourists creates the necessary funds to improve the infrastructure, education and health of the poor.
- It employs many women, which contributes to gender equality and women empowerment in developing countries.
- Locally owned small businesses benefit as they are supported by tourists, especially in rural areas.
- Tourism leads to employment diversification, which reduces the vulnerability of the poor.
- As tourism is the fastest-growing industry, more poor people are likely to benefit from it.
- Tourism provides a number of jobs that require no formal training, which reduces the cost to the poor.
- The poor are able to provide tourism products built from natural resources and cultural heritage.
- The poor are able to supply formal businesses with goods that are sold to tourists, e.g. curio shops.
- Tourism employs a high proportion of youth under the age of 25, which can be used as a stepping stone to better opportunities.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(Allocate a maximum of 2 marks for a mere listing of facts/examples.)

subQuestions.questionText: With the aid of a correctly labelled graph, explain maximum prices as a consequence of market failure.
subQuestions.memoText:
Memo answer (8 marks):

Graph requirements (max 4 marks):
- Correct labelling of the axes (PRICE on y-axis, QUANTITY on x-axis) = 1 mark
- Correct labelling on the axes (P/R20, P1/R15, Q1/100, Q/150, Q2/200) = 1 mark
- Correct drawing and labelling of curves (D demand and S supply intersecting at equilibrium B) = 1 mark
- Indication of maximum price (horizontal line at P1/R15 below equilibrium) = 1 mark

Explanation (max 4 marks):
- The government sets a maximum price (ceiling) below the market price to make goods more affordable.
- Maximum prices allow the poor greater access to certain goods and services.
- Initially the market equilibrium price is P/R20 and equilibrium quantity is Q/150.
- The government intervenes and passes a law that products cannot be sold for more than P1/R15.
- The effect of this maximum price is that quantity supplied decreases to Q1/100 and quantity demanded increases to Q2/200.
- Maximum prices may cause a shortage of goods in the economy; however, they improve the welfare of some consumers since goods can be purchased at reasonable prices.
- Black markets develop because producers may want to charge higher prices than the maximum prices.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(Allocate a maximum of 4 marks for a mere listing of facts/examples.)

subQuestions.questionText: How can the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) use the monetary policy to combat inflation?
subQuestions.memoText:
Memo answer (8 marks):
- The SARB can curb inflation by increasing the repo rate, which makes it expensive to borrow money.
- Banks pass on the increased cost of borrowing (repo rate) to their clients by increasing the interest rate.
- High interest rates discourage consumers from taking unnecessary credit, discouraging consumer spending.
- The SARB can directly decrease the supply of money by selling government securities in the open market.
- Commercial banks are required to hold a certain minimum cash reserve with the central bank.
- An increase in the cash reserve requirement limits the amount of money that banks can give out as credit and helps to curb inflation.
- The SARB can persuade commercial banks to act in a responsible manner when granting credit under inflationary conditions.
- Moral suasion helps to reduce inflation because credit will be granted to fewer consumers.
- The SARB can revaluate the value of the currency, which will result in more imported goods into the country, thereby increasing aggregate supply.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(Allocate a maximum of 2 marks for a mere listing of facts/examples.)

questions.title: QUESTION 5: MICROECONOMICS (Essay â€” Section C, choose one of Q5 or Q6)

subQuestions.questionText: Examine the characteristics of monopoly in detail. (26 marks) How does the existence of monopolies cause a challenge to the various role players in the economy? (10 marks) [40]
subQuestions.memoText:
Memo essay rubric and content:

INTRODUCTION (Max 2 marks):
Monopoly exists where there is only one seller of a product, where the product has no close substitutes, and where barriers block entry into the market completely. (Accept any other correct relevant introduction.)

BODY â€” MAIN PART (Max 26 marks):

Number of firms/businesses:
- The monopolist is the only supplier of a product, which implies that there is no competition in this market structure.
- The monopoly is also responsible for the industry's total output, e.g. De Beers and Eskom.

Nature of product:
- The product is unique and has no close substitutes, which implies that consumers' choice is limited.
- The product has relatively inelastic demand, meaning quantity demanded is less responsive to price changes.

Market entry:
- Refers to how easy or difficult it is for businesses to enter or leave the market.
- Market entry into a monopoly is entirely/completely blocked.
- Barriers include: high development costs, limited size of the market, exclusive ownership of raw materials, patents, licensing, sole rights, import restrictions.
- Two main groups: Natural monopolies and Artificial monopolies.

Natural monopolies:
- High development costs are frequently a reason for the existence of natural monopolies.
- Provision of electricity is an example because building power stations and transmission lines costs billions of rand.
- Often owned or regulated by government and can serve the whole market at a lower price than two or more businesses together.

Artificial monopolies:
- Exist due to non-economic barriers to entry, such as patents.
- A patent is the legal and exclusive right of a patent holder to manufacture a product using his/her unique invention.
- Licences also create artificial monopolies. In SA, licences are required for radio/TV broadcasting, telephone and cellular communication networks, and commercial production of electricity.

Control over price:
- A monopolist has full control over the market price and is regarded as a price maker.
- Can decide on price-quantity combinations on the demand curve.
- Possibility of consumer exploitation; may restrict output to charge a higher price.
- Limited by market demand: monopolist does not control demand.
- Consumers have limited budgets, so a monopoly cannot charge excessive prices.
- The monopolist's product still competes for consumers' favour with all other products.

Market information:
- All buyers and the single seller have full knowledge about current market conditions.
- High degree of transparency; no incentive to hide information.

Demand curve:
- A monopolist faces a normal downward-sloping demand curve.
- Demand is relatively inelastic because the product has no close substitutes.
- Demand curve = average revenue curve.
- Marginal revenue is less than price, so the MR curve lies below the demand curve.

Economic profit/loss:
- Can earn economic profit or loss in the short run.
- If making a loss in the short run, will build a new plant for profit in the long run.
- If making a profit in the short run, will expand capacity for more profit in the long run.

Decision making:
- Makes decisions independently because there are no competitors.
- Decisions may be influenced by government laws and regulations, e.g. NERSA influences Eskom's decisions.

Collusion:
- Irrelevant because there is one business in the market.

Productive and allocative efficiency:
- Does not achieve productive efficiency: output is not produced at minimum average cost.
- Allocative inefficiency: output does not correspond with quantity demanded by consumers.
- Monopoly produces output where price is above marginal cost.

(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(Allocate a maximum of 8 marks for headings and examples.)

ADDITIONAL PART (Max 10 marks): Challenges caused by monopolies:
- Monopolies produce where prices exceed marginal costs, charging higher prices above market equilibrium.
- Barriers to entry prevent new businesses from entering, stifling competition and limiting consumer choice.
- Consumers are manipulated through aggressive advertising to create false needs.
- Market failure: monopolies reduce consumer surplus, leaving few consumers able to afford goods/services.
- Consumers may pay higher prices for inferior quality goods due to no close substitutes.
- Monopolies raise the cost of living by charging high prices to maintain profitability.
- Government must implement policies to regulate monopolies and prevent exploitation.
- Lack of competition may lead to low quality and outdated goods/services.
- Monopolies create shortages, leading to allocative inefficiencies.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(Allocate a maximum of 2 marks for mere listing of facts.)

CONCLUSION (Max 2 marks): A monopoly fails to achieve both productive and allocative efficiency as they do not produce at the lowest possible average cost and do not produce at optimum output level. (Accept any other correct higher-order conclusion.)

TOTAL: 40 marks.

questions.title: QUESTION 6: CONTEMPORARY ECONOMIC ISSUES (Essay â€” Section C, choose one of Q5 or Q6)

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss in detail any FIVE environmental problems and the international measures taken to address these challenges. (26 marks) How can conservation and preservation help to ensure that the environment is sustained? (10 marks) [40]
subQuestions.memoText:
Memo essay rubric and content:

INTRODUCTION (Max 2 marks):
Environmental sustainability is the ability of the environment to survive its use for economic activities / Environmental issues are global issues such as pollution that affect the environment and natural resources. (Accept any other correct relevant introduction.)

BODY â€” MAIN PART (Max 26 marks): Discuss any FIVE environmental problems and international measures.

Biodiversity loss:
- The diversity of species in the world decreases rapidly due to extinction; this is irreversible.
- Modern techniques such as gene transplant can help limit species loss.
- The UN Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) prohibits trade in endangered plant and animal species.
- Monitoring and regulation of trade in endangered species is carried out using permits and quotas in South Africa.

Chemical waste:
- Chemical waste is toxic; effects on organisms can be death or infertility.
- Must be carefully managed so it does not leak into ground water.
- The Stockholm Protocol bans twelve of the deadliest manufactured chemicals.
- The Rotterdam Convention protects countries that lack adequate infrastructure to monitor the import and export of dangerous chemicals.

Hazardous waste:
- More than chemical waste â€” includes toxic metal waste such as lead.
- Has a slow decomposition rate (stays poisonous for a long time).
- Can endanger all life forms and the entire ecosystem.
- The Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Waste allows trade between countries that have signed the convention.

Climate change:
- A build-up of certain gases (e.g. carbon dioxide) in the atmosphere captures heat, leading to global warming.
- Effects include changes in temperature and weather patterns, causing destruction to plant and animal inhabitants.
- The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) sets objectives to reduce greenhouse gases.
- The Kyoto Protocol agreed greenhouse gas emission levels for developed countries.

Loss of indigenous knowledge:
- Loss of knowledge about the natural environment may result in indigenous people losing their way of making a living.
- Indigenous people use organic methods and natural processes; this knowledge may be lost to future generations.
- Local capacity building can help indigenous people learn more about the environment beyond their traditional life style.
- UNESCO's Management of Social Transformation (MOST) programme is a global effort to document local/indigenous knowledge before it is lost forever.

(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(Allocate a maximum of 8 marks for mere listing of facts/examples.)
(Accept other major environmental problems such as pollution and deforestation.)

ADDITIONAL PART (Max 10 marks): How conservation and preservation ensure environmental sustainability:
- Conservation in SA ensures sustainability by bringing balance in the ecosystem as animals and plants interact.
- Reducing greenhouse gases reaching the atmosphere decreases global warming.
- Conservation ensures management of natural resources to benefit future generations.
- Using water wisely; municipalities impose restrictions on water consumption.
- Reusing, reducing and recycling means people use fewer resources, reducing production of plastics, etc.
- Setting fishing quotas to prevent catches exceeding fish population growth.
- Setting quotas for cutting down trees to prevent deforestation exceeding the rate required.
- Ensuring food security and sustainability of animals and mountains attracts more tourists.
